<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: Small manufacturers account for more than 98 percent of U.S. manufacturing firms and employ 4.8 million Americans.\1\ They play a critical role in regional economies and in maintaining supply chain resilience. Yet many of these businesses struggle to access the capital needed to expand production and modernize operations in a rapidly changing economic landscape.
\1\Off. of Advocacy, Manufacturing Statistics 2025, U.S. Small Bus. Admin. (Mar. 2025), https://advocacy.sba.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/ 03/Manufacturing-Infographic-Series_ FINAL.pdf.
The Small Business Administration (SBA)'s flagship 7(a) loan guaranty program helps close this capital access shortage by partially guaranteeing loans made by certified-partnered lenders. The SBA also oversees the 504/Certified Development Company (CDC) loan guaranty program, in which private, nonprofit corporations provide SBA-guaranteed long-term, fixed-rate loans for major fixed assets such as land, structures, machinery, and equipment.\2\
\2\Cong. Research Serv., Small Business Administration: A Primer on Programs and Funding 15 (Apr. 27, 2022).
The 7(a) and 504/CDC programs are both intended to be zero-subsidy, meaning that the costs of administering the program should be covered by the fees that the SBA receives for processing guarantees. However, recent data indicates a concerning rise in defaults on 7(a) loans.\3\ When defaults rise, the SBA must spend more of taxpayers' money on reimbursing 7(a) lenders for much of the losses incurred, threatening the zero-subsidy and the program's ability to pay for itself.
\3\U.S. Small Bus. Admin., FY 2024 7(a) Program Risk Analysis 16 (Dec. 1, 2024).
The SBA is required by law to send an annual 7(a) Program Risk Analysis report (the Report) to the House Committee on Small Business and the Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship.\4\ The most recent report provided to both the Majority and Democratic staffs, for Fiscal Year 2024, highlights that early default rate (i.e. the default rate for loans not older than one year) rose significantly from slightly over 0.2 percent in June 2022 to 1.01 percent in June 2024.\5\ The report also demonstrates that the last 12-month default rate (i.e. the default rate for loans older than one year) rose from 1.32 percent in June 2022 to 2.76 percent in June 2024.\6\ Additionally, data provided to Democratic staff from an outside industry consultant studying the 7(a) program demonstrates that that the overall default rate in the 7(a) program is continuing to rise an alarming rate.\7\ According to the most recent data compiled by this industry consultant, the default rate in the overall 7(a) program is approximately 3.7 percent as of October 2024.\8\
\4\15 USC Sec. 657t (h)(2).
\5\U.S. Small Bus. Admin., supra note 3, at 16.
\6\Id.
\7\On file with the H. Comm. on Small Bus. Democrats. Data is available for review upon request.
\8\Id.
Perhaps more alarming is the fact that 7(a) loans originated to small manufacturers have amongst the highest level of defaults in the entire program. Specifically, the SBA report states ``(c)onstruction and (m)anufacturing continue to demonstrate higher levels of risk than the overall 7(a) portfolio, with increases in Stressed Loan Rate, Early Default Loan Rate, and Last 12-Month Default Rate from June 30, 2023, to June 30, 2024.''\9\ The early default rate for manufacturers rose from 0.16 percent in June 2022 to 1 percent in June 2024.\10\ Similarly, the last 12-month default rate for manufacturers rose from slightly over 2 percent in June 2022 to 3.13 percent in June 2024.\11\ In other words, loans to manufacturers are one of the most challenging elements of the 7(a) loan portfolio, which a loan level increase would exacerbate.
\9\U.S. Small Bus. Admin., supra note 3, at 7.
\10\Id, at 21.
\11\Id, at 22.
The recent spike in 7(a) loan defaults has been driven in part by the larger monetary environment. Interest rates rose in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic to help combat rising inflation.\12\ However, these rate increases also impacted the size of regular interest payments required of 7(a) borrowers (among others), and with higher interest payments, more borrowers became unable to make full payments.
\12\Federal Funds Effective Rate, Fed. Rsrv. Bank of St. Louis (Jun. 2025), https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FEDFUNDS.
Unlike the 7(a) program, the 504/CDC program does not have problems with the rising number of loan defaults; the 504/CDC program has not required a subsidy from a congressional appropriation since Fiscal Year 2015.\13\
\13\Cong. Research Serv., Small Business Administration 504/CDC Loan Guaranty Program (Jun. 16, 2022); Pub. L. No. 117-328, Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023, 136 Stat. 4459 (Dec. 29, 2022); Pub. L. No. 118-47, Further Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024, 138 Stat. 460 (Mar. 23, 2024).
As of June 30, 2025, more than $27.6 billion in loan approvals have already been issued, out of the program's $35 billion cap for FY 2025. If the loan approvals continue at the same rate, it's estimated the 7(a) program would reach its authorized limit before the end of the fiscal year. I am concerned that increasing the loan limit for the manufacturing sector could lead to those larger loans consuming a disproportionate share of the program's overall level of lending authority, making it harder for the smallest of the small businesses to obtain 7(a) loans.
As I've stated, I am open to a discussion on increasing loan caps for manufacturers in the 504/CDC program and Committee staff has expressed that position to the majority staff on multiple occasions. That said, strong concerns persist that increasing the loan level for 7(a) loans at this time would expose taxpayers, lenders, and borrowers to unnecessarily elevated levels of risk, threatening the integrity of the 7(a) program. Committee Democrats have repeatedly expressed these concerns and shared related data with the Majority, but the Majority has refused to consider modifying or removing this bill's 7(a) provisions. As such, the loan level increases to the 7(a) program currently in H.R. 3174 remain far too imprudent to earn my support.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.
